book_title: Chapter 1: From Hyderabad Lab Bench to Global CRDMO
question: How did a 1999 Hyderabad medicinal chemistry startup evolve into an integrated global CRDMO, and what drove its multi-year revenue and margin cycles?

epigraph.quote: We are seeing customer engagements evolve from individual projects into larger, more strategic relationships spanning discovery, development, and manufacturing.
epigraph.author: Krishna Kanumuri, Managing Director & CEO, Sai Life Sciences

web_blocks.title: 1999 Founding and the Early Medicinal Chemistry Wedge

web_blocks.html: Sai Life Sciences Limited was founded in 1999 in Hyderabad by Dr. Kanumuri Ranga Raju and his son Krishna Kanumuri, now MD and CEO [3]. Back then, Indian pharma outsourcing focused mostly on generic active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and low-cost intermediates. Sai Life chose a different path. It focused 100% on innovator drugmakers in regulated US, European, and Japanese markets rather than generic price wars [17].

The firm started with custom synthetic chemistry and early medicinal chemistry. It helped global drugmakers build novel small-molecule libraries faster and cheaper than Western labs. Over its first fifteen years, Sai Life added in vitro and in vivo biology, DMPK, process chemistry, and cGMP API production. It bought and upgraded cGMP plants at IDA Bollaram (Unit III) and built its main large-scale API campus at Bidar (Unit IV) in Karnataka [19]. By avoiding generic price wars and building audit-ready quality early, Sai Life positioned itself to grow alongside its clients' drugs.

web_blocks.title: Private Equity Catalysis: HBM Healthcare (2014) and TPG Capital (2018)

web_blocks.html: Moving from a mid-sized Indian CRO to a global Contract Research, Development, and Manufacturing Organization (CRDMO) took more capital than internal cash could fund. In 2014, Swiss healthcare investor HBM Healthcare Investments backed Sai Life [5]. In 2018, global private equity firm TPG Capital bought a major stake, reaching ~39% pre-IPO [5]. TPG brought both growth capital and global pharma boardroom ties.

With TPG and HBM behind it, Sai Life launched the SaiNxt program from 2018 to 2023 and spent over US$150 million [22]. Rather than keeping all scientists in India, SaiNxt opened two Western R&D hubs. One is an exploratory biology lab in Watertown (Greater Boston, Massachusetts). The other is a Process R&D and Kilo-scale lab at Alderley Park in Manchester, UK [19]. At the same time, Sai Life expanded its Genome Valley R&D campus (Unit II, Hyderabad) and upgraded Bidar with automated hydrogenation and OEB 6 HPAPI suites [19, 22]. This dual-shore model solved a key biotech pain point: keeping early biology near Cambridge and Europe while transferring scale-up cleanly to India.

web_blocks.title: The FY20–FY24 Investment Trough vs. the FY25–FY27 Operating Inflection

web_blocks.html: The US$150 million+ SaiNxt buildout created a sharp earnings cycle. From FY19 to FY22, revenue grew modestly from ₹695 Cr to ₹870 Cr, while operating profit margin (OPM) fell from 25% in FY19 to 15% in FY22 and 14% in FY23 [1]. Depreciation more than doubled from ₹44 Cr in FY19 to ₹99 Cr in FY23 [1]. Borrowings jumped from ₹249 Cr to ₹933 Cr as Boston, Manchester, Hyderabad, and Bidar opened ahead of full utilization [1]. Net profit bottomed at ₹6 Cr in FY22 and ₹10 Cr in FY23, and ROCE dropped to 3% in FY22 [1]. Tighter global biotech funding in 2022–2023 also slowed early discovery starts.

From FY24 onward, operating leverage took over as innovator drugs moved into late-stage clinical and commercial supply. Revenue jumped +40% in FY23 (₹1,217 Cr), +20% in FY24 (₹1,465 Cr), +16% in FY25 (₹1,695 Cr), and +29% in FY26 (₹2,192 Cr) [1, 6]. OPM rebounded from 14% in FY23 to 20% in FY24, 24% in FY25, and 29% in FY26 (28% in H1 FY27) [1, 8]. In December 2024, Sai Life raised ₹3,043 Cr in its IPO—a ₹950 Cr fresh issue to cut debt and a ₹2,093 Cr Offer for Sale by TPG, HBM, and promoters—and listed on NSE and BSE on December 18, 2024 [4].

Commercial Scale, TPG Exit & Credit Upgrade

FY26 sales ₹2,192 Cr (+29%), PAT ₹349 Cr; H1 FY27 sales ₹1,213 Cr (+17%), 34 commercial NCEs, 700 KL active Bidar base (+225 KL block in quality trials); TPG exited fully (Aug 2025); Ind-Ra upgraded to IND AA/Stable (Nov 2026) [1, 8, 27, 30, 31].
web_blocks.takeaway: Sai Life absorbed a multi-year margin and return trough (FY21–FY23) to build Western discovery hubs and Bidar commercial scale, deleveraged via its Dec 2024 IPO, cleared TPG's PE overhang by Aug 2025, and earned an IND AA/Stable credit upgrade in Nov 2026 [1, 4, 27, 31].

web_blocks.title: Why the Dec 2024 IPO & Aug 2025 TPG Exit Were Structural Turning Points
paragraphs: Unlike pure-OFS private equity exits, Sai Life's ₹950 Cr fresh issue (100% utilized as per CRISIL's monitoring report: ₹720 Cr debt repayment and ₹190 Cr general corporate purposes) directly repaired the balance sheet. Borrowings fell from ₹928 Cr in Mar 2024 to ₹288 Cr in Mar 2026, halving annual interest cost from ₹88 Cr in FY24 to ₹41 Cr in FY26 [1, 4]. Following a June 2025 tranche, TPG Asia completely exited its remaining 14.72% stake via a ₹2,675 Cr block deal in August 2025, removing the primary PE selling overhang as DIIs (32.32%) and FIIs (19.91%) stepped in [1, 31].

However, the firm has now entered an aggressive FY27 capex wave. Management guides ₹1,100–₹1,300 Cr for FY27 and incurred ₹621 Cr in H1 FY27 (₹561 Cr cash capex), lifting Sep 2026 borrowings (including ₹171 Cr lease liabilities) back to ₹620 Cr—mostly short-term debt—before India Ratings upgraded facilities to IND AA/Stable (Nov 13, 2026) and rated ₹100 Cr of new bank term loans on Nov 24, 2026 [1, 27, 28, 29].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Sai Life Sciences without getting swept up in market noise, you and I have to start in 1999 in Hyderabad. At a time when almost every ambitious Indian chemical entrepreneur was chasing the fast cash of generic active pharmaceutical ingredients, Dr. Kanumuri Ranga Raju and his son Krishna Kanumuri made a contrarian bet: they would not sell a single generic pill or commodity API. Instead, they built a contract research bench exclusively for innovator pharmaceutical and biotech companies in the United States, Europe, and Japan.

Why was that decision so consequential? Because generic APIs compete on brute-force cost per kilogram once patents expire, whereas innovator drug discovery and development compete on speed, intellectual property trust, and regulatory precision. For the first fifteen years, Sai Life was a disciplined but relatively modest synthetic chemistry partner. It helped Western drug hunters make novel molecules during early discovery and gradually added process development and cGMP manufacturing in Bollaram and Bidar.

Yet by the mid-2010s, management realized a hard structural truth: Indian CROs that stayed purely on the discovery side remained trapped in low-margin headcount arbitrage, while pure-play manufacturers without early discovery relationships struggled to win high-value innovator molecules before competitors locked them in. To capture the full lifecycle of a drug, Sai Life needed both halves of the bridge—plus a physical presence inside Western biotech clusters.

That realization set off two transformative private equity partnerships—first with Swiss specialist HBM Healthcare Investments in 2014, and then with global buyout giant TPG Capital in 2018. Armed with institutional capital, Krishna Kanumuri launched SaiNxt, a US$150 million-plus overhaul between 2018 and 2023. You can see the ambition of SaiNxt in the geography alone: Sai Life planted an exploratory biology lab right inside the Greater Boston biotech cluster in Watertown and a process R&D hub at Alderley Park in Manchester, UK, linking them directly to a modernized R&D campus in Hyderabad's Genome Valley and commercial reactors in Bidar.

Every heavy industrial buildout extracts a toll before it pays a dividend, and Sai Life's income statement between FY20 and FY23 is a textbook case study. As depreciation climbed from ₹44 crore in FY19 to ₹99 crore in FY23 and debt swelled from ₹249 crore to ₹933 crore, operating margins collapsed from 25% to 14%, and net profit nearly vanished to ₹6 crore in FY22. To a casual observer looking only at trailing numbers in 2023, Sai Life looked like a capital-heavy, low-return contractor. In reality, those labs and reactors were filling up with late-phase clinical assets and integrated pharma partnerships.

When the operating inflection arrived in FY24 through FY26, it was dramatic: revenue climbed from ₹1,217 crore in FY23 to ₹2,192 crore in FY26, operating margins more than doubled back to 29%, and the December 2024 IPO injected ₹950 crore of fresh equity to wipe out most of the legacy debt. By August 2025, TPG Asia had completely exited its remaining 14.72% stake via block deals absorbed by domestic and foreign institutions, removing the private equity overhang while India Ratings upgraded Sai Life's credit profile to IND AA/Stable in November 2026. Today, as you and I examine the business in late November 2026, Sai Life stands at the start of its next capex wave—guiding ₹1,100 to ₹1,300 crore of capital spending in FY27 alone, initially bridged with short-term borrowings—testing whether management can compound scale without repeating the margin compression of 2022.

book_subsections.title: The Two-Cycle Pattern You Must Remember
paragraphs: When you study contract manufacturers, you quickly learn that capacity always precedes revenue by eighteen to thirty-six months. You have to hire PhD chemists, qualify cleanrooms, and pass USFDA inspections long before a client's Phase III drug wins commercial approval and orders multi-ton batches. Sai Life's first cycle—SaiNxt—took borrowings to ₹933 crore and crushed ROE into single digits before Bidar and Hyderabad filled up.

Its second cycle is underway right now in FY27, with ₹621 crore already incurred in the first half (₹561 crore cash capex) and consolidated borrowings ticking back up from ₹288 crore to ₹620 crore by September 2026—including ₹418 crore of short-term borrowings alongside ₹171 crore of lease liabilities. The difference this time is the earnings base and credit standing: instead of generating ₹169 crore of EBITDA as it did in FY23, Sai Life now generates nearly ₹700 crore of trailing twelve-month EBITDA and holds an IND AA/Stable credit rating, though management must still term out short-term debt and keep commercial molecule ramp-ups on schedule.

book_subsections.title: Governance & Institutionalization Post-IPO
paragraphs: Notice how cleanly the shareholder register institutionalized after December 2024. After partially monetizing in the ₹2,093 crore IPO Offer for Sale, TPG Asia sold down its remaining holdings in June and August 2025—exiting its final 14.72% block for roughly ₹2,675 crore—eliminating the main private equity supply overhang. Meanwhile, promoters retained 34.50% ownership with zero pledged shares and zero open-market selling (the slight drift from 35.23% in December 2024 reflects recurring employee ESOP allotments, including 7.47 lakh shares issued in FY27 through November 5, 2026), while institutional DIIs (32.32%) and FIIs (19.91%) stepped in to own more than 52% combined by September 2026. In November 2026, the board also bolstered senior leadership by appointing a veteran Head of Quality & Regulatory Affairs from Dr. Reddy's and Novartis.

book_subsections.title: Why the Post-IPO Ownership Shift Changes Quarterly Expectations
paragraphs: Before December 2024, Sai Life Sciences answered to two patient private equity boards—HBM Healthcare and TPG Capital—who were willing to absorb a three-year margin trough from 25% down to 14% while Boston, Manchester, and Bidar were under construction. Public equity markets rarely extend that same patience without clear communication. When quarterly depreciation steps up on a ₹1,100 to ₹1,300 crore capex wave, public investors immediately scrutinize whether utilization is lagging or leading.

That is why the shift in the shareholder register matters so much to our fundamental thesis. With promoters holding 34.50%, TPG fully exited, and domestic and foreign institutions holding over 52% by September 2026, Sai Life has graduated into an institutional mid-cap bellwether. The operational discipline required to run multi-year pharmaceutical programs hasn't changed, but the tolerance for uncommunicated working-capital, short-term debt, or CWIP surprises is far lower today than it was under private ownership.

book_subsections.title: Why Dual-Shore Geography Is Harder to Copy Than Reactors
paragraphs: Anyone with ₹500 crore and a bank loan can buy stainless-steel reactors and install glass-lined vessels in an industrial park. What takes a decade of cultural patience to build is a bilingual scientific organization where a PhD medicinal chemist in Watertown or Manchester can hand a synthetic route to a process engineer in Hyderabad on a Friday evening and see analytical data on Monday morning.

That cultural and scientific bridge is the real legacy of the SaiNxt years. When Western biotech founders visit Genome Valley or Bidar, they are not auditing a low-cost outsourcing vendor; they are inspecting an extension of their own CMC organization. That trust is what turned a modest 1999 chemistry shop into a partner for 18 of the top 25 global pharmaceutical companies.

book_subsections.title: How the 2018–2023 Capex Trough Built Today's Competitive Moat
paragraphs: It is worth pausing on how unusual Sai Life's pre-IPO investment cycle really was. Most private-equity-backed Indian manufacturers starve capital expenditure in the three years before an IPO so that trailing EBITDA margins and return on equity look artificially polished for retail roadshows. Sai Life and TPG did the exact opposite: they spent more than US$150 million between 2018 and 2023, watched net profit shrink to ₹6 crore in FY22, and waited until utilization and margins inflected in FY24 and FY25 before listing.

That sequence tells you something important about promoter mentality. Dr. Ranga Raju and Krishna Kanumuri were willing to look temporarily unprofitable in order to build permanent Western client interfaces in Watertown and Manchester alongside commercial reactors in Bidar. Now that the company is public, that same long-horizon mindset is driving the ₹1,100 to ₹1,300 crore FY27 expansion.

book_subsections.title: Why Promoter Continuity Matters Through Heavy Capex Cycles
paragraphs: One quiet strength in Sai Life's history is leadership continuity. Dr. Kanumuri Ranga Raju founded the company in 1999, and Krishna Kanumuri has steered it through both the SaiNxt transformation and the December 2024 IPO. Having founder-scientists who lived through the FY22–FY23 margin trough still holding 34.5% equity reduces the risk of reckless empire-building during the FY27 Choutuppal buildout.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: History in the CRDMO sector rarely moves in straight lines. Sai Life's 14% operating margin trough in FY23 was not a broken business—it was the predictable depreciation and staffing drag of building Boston, Manchester, and Bidar ahead of commercial demand. The real discipline for us as analysts is separating temporary investment troughs from permanent capital destruction.
